domain:
    i: dim in [0, N)        # row index of C, A, B
    j: dim in [0, N)        # column index of C
    k: dim in [0, M)        # shared inner dimension

data:
    # All matrices are stored in conventional row-major layout.
    # C is N x N, A and B are N x M.
    A[i, k]: in  DATA_TYPE = (i, k) -> i * M + k   # row-major (N rows, M cols)
    B[i, k]: in  DATA_TYPE = (i, k) -> i * M + k   # row-major (N rows, M cols)
    C[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j # row-major (N rows, N cols)

parameters:
    alpha: DATA_TYPE
    beta:  DATA_TYPE
    # The following are tunable constants for the optimization (compile-time or run-time tunables).
    T_I: int   # tile size in i-dimension, e.g. 64
    T_J: int   # tile size in j-dimension, e.g. 64
    T_K: int   # tile size in k-dimension, e.g. 32
    V:   int   # vector width in j-dimension, e.g. 8 or 16 elements
    U:   int   # unroll factor for k-tiles, e.g. 4

computation:
    # Symmetric rank-2k update on the lower triangle of C:
    #
    # Original kernel:
    #   for i in 0..N-1:
    #     for j in 0..i:
    #       C[i][j] *= beta
    #     for k in 0..M-1:
    #       for j in 0..i:
    #         C[i][j] += alpha*A[j][k]*B[i][k] + alpha*B[j][k]*A[i][k]
    #
    # Algebraically fused and with alpha factored out of the k-sum:
    for i, j:
        if j <= i:
            C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j] +
                      alpha * sum(k, A[j, k] * B[i, k] +
                                     B[j, k] * A[i, k])
        # For j > i, C[i,j] is left unchanged (upper triangle passes original values through).

optimization:
    # 1. Exploit the triangular structure logically while keeping a regular loop nest.
    #    We keep rectangular loops over (i,j) and a branch "if j <= i" rather than
    #    changing the data layout of C, so that the upper triangle remains stored and
    #    readable exactly as in the original program.
    #
    #    (The compiler is free to derive an equivalent triangular iteration space,
    #     but the semantics are defined via the if-condition above.)

    # 2. Arithmetic optimization: factor alpha outside the k-sum.
    #    This is already reflected in the computation section:
    #        C[i,j] += alpha * sum_k( A[j,k]*B[i,k] + B[j,k]*A[i,k] )
    #    rather than
    #        C[i,j] += sum_k( alpha*A[j,k]*B[i,k] + alpha*B[j,k]*A[i,k] )
    #    which reduces multiplications by alpha from O(N^2 * M) to O(N^2).

    # 3. Loop blocking (tiling) for cache locality.
    #
    #    We tile the spatial (i,j) domain and the reduction dimension k, so that
    #    each (I,J) tile of C is updated using a sequence of smaller K-tiles.
    #    This keeps stripes of A and B in cache while updating a small block of C.
    block(i, I, T_I)   # i = I * T_I + i_inner
    block(j, J, T_J)   # j = J * T_J + j_inner
    block(k, K, T_K)   # k = K * T_K + k_inner

    # 4. Loop reordering to improve memory access patterns.
    #
    #    Within a spatial tile (I,J), we iterate i_inner outer, j_inner inner,
    #    and perform the full reduction over k inside the (i_inner,j_inner) loop,
    #    so that a single C[i,j] element is accumulated in registers and written once.
    #
    #    Conceptual order inside a tile:
    #      for i_inner:
    #        for j_inner:
    #          if j <= i:
    #            acc = 0
    #            for K:
    #              for k_inner:
    #                acc += A[j,k] * B[i,k] + B[j,k] * A[i,k]
    #            C[i,j] = beta*C[i,j] + alpha*acc
    #
    #    This corresponds to hoisting the tile indices outermost and placing K
    #    just inside (i_inner,j_inner); we then hoist tiles explicitly:
    hoist(I)   # make I (tile of i) outermost
    hoist(J)   # then J (tile of j)
    hoist(K)   # then K (tile of k) outside the inner (i,j) micro-kernel

    # 5. Keep j as the innermost spatial dimension for contiguous C access.
    #
    #    Inside each (I,J) tile and for a fixed row i, C[i,j] is stored
    #    contiguously along j. We therefore maintain j_inner as the innermost
    #    spatial loop and only move K relative to i_inner/j_inner as needed.
    #    If the default inner order after tiling is (K, i_inner, j_inner),
    #    interchange K and j_inner so that C accesses are unit-stride:
    interchange(J, K)   # ensure inner order ... i_inner, K, j_inner -> i_inner, j_inner, K

    # 6. Vectorization.
    #
    #    Vectorize along j (columns) inside a tile, since C[i,*], A[j,*], and B[j,*]
    #    are laid out row-major and we are iterating j with unit stride. The
    #    triangular condition j <= i becomes a masked vector operation.
    vectorize(J, V)

    # 7. Unrolling of the inner k-tile for better ILP.
    #
    #    Within each K tile, unroll the k_inner loop by a small factor U to
    #    expose instruction-level parallelism in the dot products:
    unroll(K, U)

    # 8. Parallelization across outer tiles in i (rows of C).
    #
    #    Rows of C are independent given that C is only updated at (i,j) with
    #    j <= i, so tiles along I can be executed in parallel with no write
    #    conflicts. We parallelize at the tile level for good granularity.
    parallelize(I)

    # 9. Optional: software prefetching / small temporaries (not expressed in DSL).
    #    An implementation may additionally:
    #      - allocate small on-chip / stack buffers to hold a K×T_J slab of A and B
    #        for each i-tile, reusing them while iterating over j,
    #      - prefetch upcoming A[i,*] and B[i,*] rows.
    #    These use only O(T_I * T_J + T_I * T_K + T_J * T_K) extra elements,
    #    staying well within the 50% memory overhead guideline.

domain:
    i: dim in [0, N)      # row index of C, A, B
    j: dim in [0, N)      # column index of C (only j <= i is updated)
    k: dim in [0, M)      # inner dimension over columns of A,B

data:
    # Original C layout:
    #   C[n][n], A[n][m], B[n][m], all row-major.
    # We model that directly.
    A[i, k]: in  num_t = (i, k) -> i * M + k   # N x M, row-major
    B[i, k]: in  num_t = (i, k) -> i * M + k   # N x M, row-major
    C[i, j]: inout num_t = (i, j) -> i * N + j # N x N, row-major; only lower triangle is modified

parameters:
    alpha: num_t
    beta:  num_t

    # Tuning knobs for optimization (chosen per target machine)
    TI: int   # tile size in i (rows of C), e.g. 64
    TJ: int   # tile size in j (cols of C), e.g. 64
    TK: int   # tile size in k (reduction dim), e.g. 32
    VJ: int   # SIMD width for vectorization along j, e.g. 8 (float/AVX2), 4 (double/AVX2)
    UK: int   # unroll factor for k inside a TK-tile, e.g. 4 or 8 (UK | TK)

computation:
    # Scale C’s lower triangle by beta.
    # Matches:
    #   for (i = 0..N-1)
    #     for (j = 0..i)
    #       C[i][j] *= beta;
    for i in seq([0, N)):
        for j in [0, i]:
            C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j]

    # Rank-2k symmetric update:
    #   C[i][j] += alpha*A[j][k]*B[i][k] + alpha*B[j][k]*A[i][k]
    # for j <= i only. Upper triangle (j > i) is left unchanged.
    for i in seq([0, N)):
        for j in [0, i]:
            C[i, j] = C[i, j] +
                      alpha * sum(k in [0, M),
                                  A[j, k] * B[i, k] +
                                  B[j, k] * A[i, k])

optimization:
    # ------------ High-level strategy ------------
    #  - Preserve triangular domain (j <= i) to avoid redundant work.
    #  - Tile i,j,k for cache locality.
    #  - Parallelize over outer tiles of i (independent row bands of C).
    #  - Vectorize over contiguous j inside tiles.
    #  - Partially unroll k to expose ILP and reduce loop overhead.
    #  - Rely on compiler to hoist A[i,k], B[i,k] across inner j-loop.

    # ------------ Blocking (tiling) ------------
    # Tile i and j so that a tile of C and corresponding rows of A,B
    # fit in shared caches (L2/L3). Tile k so that reused slices of A,B
    # fit in L1/L2.
    block(i, I, TI)      # i = I * TI + i_in, tiles of TI rows of C
    block(j, J, TJ)      # j = J * TJ + j_in, tiles of TJ cols of C
    block(k, K, TK)      # k = K * TK + k_in, tiles of TK elements in reduction

    # Order tiles to improve reuse of A,B across j within the same (I, K).
    # Outer structure: I (row tiles of C) → K (reduction tiles) → J (column tiles).
    hoist(I)             # I outermost
    hoist(K)             # iterate reduction tiles K outside of J
    hoist(J)             # column tiles J inside each (I,K)

    # Inside each (I,J,K) tile, keep the logical order:
    #   i_in (rows in tile) outer,
    #   k_in (reduction) middle/inner,
    #   j_in (columns in tile) innermost.
    # This preserves unit-stride accesses:
    #   - A[j,k] and B[j,k] are contiguous in k for fixed j,
    #   - A[i,k] and B[i,k] are contiguous in k for fixed i,
    #   - C[i,j] is contiguous in j for fixed i.

    # ------------ Exploit triangular structure ------------
    # Within each (I,J) tile and row i, we only process j <= i,
    # as in the original algorithm. Instead of a runtime branch,
    # we constrain the j-loop bounds:
    #
    #   for I in [0, ceil(N/TI)):
    #     for i in [I*TI, min(I*TI+TI, N)):
    #       maxJ = floor(i / TJ)
    #       for J in [0, maxJ]:
    #         j_lo = J * TJ
    #         j_hi = min(J * TJ + TJ, i + 1)
    #         for j in [j_lo, j_hi):
    #           ...
    #
    # This removes the inner "if (j <= i)" while preserving semantics.
    # (Expressed here as a comment; the effect is a triangular iteration
    # space inside the blocked loops.)

    # ------------ Parallelism ------------
    # Parallelize across outer row tiles I. Each I processes a disjoint
    # band of rows of C, so there are no write conflicts.
    parallelize(I)

    # Optionally, for very large N and small TI, we could also
    # parallelize over (I,J) tiles (2D tiling of C), but I-only
    # parallelism usually suffices on a 32-core CPU.

    # ------------ Vectorization ------------
    # Vectorize along j within each tile, since C[i,j] is unit-stride in j.
    # This produces SIMD loads/stores to C and SIMD-friendly accesses to
    # A[j,k], B[j,k] when TJ is a multiple of VJ.
    vectorize(j, VJ)

    # ------------ Unrolling of the reduction ------------
    # Unroll the inner k loop partially to expose more ILP and reduce
    # branch/loop overhead. UK should divide TK.
    unroll(k, UK)

    # Conceptually, inside each (I, K, i) tile:
    #
    #   for k_in in [0, TK) step UK:
    #     # scalar temps reused across all j in the tile
    #     for u in [0, UK):
    #       aa[u] = A[i, K*TK + k_in + u]
    #       bb[u] = B[i, K*TK + k_in + u]
    #     for J, j_in:
    #       j = J*TJ + j_in
    #       if j <= i:
    #         for u in [0, UK):
    #           C[i,j] += alpha * (A[j, K*TK + k_in + u] * bb[u] +
    #                              B[j, K*TK + k_in + u] * aa[u])
    #
    # The unroll(k, UK) plus standard scalar-replacement optimizations
    # lets the compiler realize this pattern without extra arrays.

    # ------------ Memory layout choices ------------
    # Keep A and B as N x M row-major:
    #   addr(A[i,k]) = base_A + i*M + k
    #   addr(B[i,k]) = base_B + i*M + k
    # so accesses A[row, k] and B[row, k] are unit-stride in the
    # innermost k-loop.
    #
    # Keep C as N x N row-major:
    #   addr(C[i,j]) = base_C + i*N + j
    # so vectorization along j is efficient.
    #
    # No additional large temporary buffers are introduced; only
    # register-resident scalars are used for hoisted A[i,k], B[i,k],
    # keeping total memory usage within the original footprint.

domain:
    i: dim in [0, N)          # row index
    j: dim in [0, N)          # col index
    k: dim in [0, M)          # reduction index

data:
    # Original arrays are row-major: A[n][m], B[n][m], C[n][n].
    # We model them in the natural (row, col) order.
    A[i, k]: in DATA_TYPE  = (i, k) -> i * M + k   # row-major N x M
    B[i, k]: in DATA_TYPE  = (i, k) -> i * M + k   # row-major N x M
    C[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j # row-major N x N, only j <= i updated (lower triangle)

parameters:
    alpha: DATA_TYPE
    beta:  DATA_TYPE

    # Tunable constants for cache/blocking and SIMD on a 32‑core x64:
    TI: int  # tile size in i (rows), e.g. 64
    TJ: int  # tile size in j (cols), e.g. 64
    TK: int  # tile size in k (reduction), e.g. 64
    VK: int  # SIMD width along k, e.g. 8 for AVX2 / 16 for AVX-512

computation:
    # --- Step 1: scale lower triangle of C by beta (upper triangle unchanged) ---
    scale:
        for i in [0, N), j in [0, N):
            if j <= i:
                C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j]

    # --- Step 2: SYR2K rank‑2k update on lower triangle ---
    #
    # Original C kernel:
    #   for (i = 0; i < N; i++) {
    #     for (j = 0; j <= i; j++)
    #       C[i][j] *= beta;
    #     for (k = 0; k < M; k++)
    #       for (j = 0; j <= i; j++) {
    #         C[i][j] += A[j][k]*alpha*B[i][k] + B[j][k]*alpha*A[i][k];
    #       }
    #   }
    #
    # Mathematically, for j <= i:
    #   C[i,j] = beta*C[i,j] + alpha * sum_k ( A[j,k]*B[i,k] + B[j,k]*A[i,k] ).
    update:
        for i in [0, N), j in [0, N):
            if j <= i:
                C[i, j] = C[i, j] +
                          alpha * sum(k in [0, M),
                                      A[j, k] * B[i, k] +
                                      B[j, k] * A[i, k])

dependencies:
    # Scaling must be done before the rank‑2k update for each (i,j) with j <= i.
    for i in [0, N), j in [0, N) with j <= i:
        scale(i, j) -> update(i, j)

optimization:
    # --- Cache blocking / tiling ---
    # Tile i (rows), j (cols), and k (reduction) to improve cache reuse:
    # Each block(I) corresponds to a tile of TI rows; i is the intra‑tile row index.
    # Same for J/TJ and K/TK.
    block(i, I, TI)    # i = I * TI + i_in
    block(j, J, TJ)    # j = J * TJ + j_in
    block(k, K, TK)    # k = K * TK + k_in

    # Hoist tile loops to the outermost level to get the global nesting:
    #   for I:
    #     for J:
    #       for K:
    #         for i_in, j_in, k_in ...
    # This yields 3D blocking over (i,j,k).
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)
    hoist(K)

    # --- Parallelism ---
    # Parallelize across independent row‑tiles. Each (I,J) tile of the lower triangle
    # updates a disjoint submatrix of C; no cross‑tile dependencies exist.
    # This exploits the 32‑core CPU.
    parallelize(I)

    # Optionally also parallelize over column tiles when N is large:
    # (Work stealing / dynamic scheduling should be used to load‑balance
    # the triangular region, but we only express the intent here.)
    # parallelize(J)

    # --- Loop ordering within a tile ---
    # Within each (I,J) tile, iterate k‑tiles (K) as the next outer loop so that:
    #   1. Rows A[j, k] and B[i, k] are streamed in k with unit stride.
    #   2. A and B tiles for a given K stay in cache while we sweep i/j in that tile.
    # This is equivalent to a blocked SYR2K similar to blocked GEMM.
    #
    # Resulting conceptual order inside each tile:
    #   for K:
    #     for i_in:
    #       for j_in:
    #         if j <= i:
    #           for k_in in [0, TK):
    #             C[i,j] += alpha * ( ... )
    interchange(K, j)   # move K outer to (i,j) pair inside the tile

    # --- Vectorization and unrolling ---
    # Vectorize along the inner reduction dimension k_in to exploit SIMD:
    # A[j,k] and B[i,k] are contiguous along k in memory (row‑major),
    # so vectorizing k gives coalesced loads and efficient dot‑product style code.
    vectorize(k, VK)

    # Unroll the remaining scalar reduction work within each TK‑sized block
    # to reduce loop overhead and enable further instruction‑level parallelism.
    unroll(k, 4)

    # Optionally unroll small intra‑tile j loops for better use of registers,
    # while the triangular condition (j <= i) still guards correctness.
    unroll(j, 4)

    # --- Notes on the triangular structure ---
    # The if (j <= i) condition is preserved inside all tiles. Blocking and
    # loop reordering may cause some iterations to execute for j > i, but
    # they are immediately discarded by the conditional, so the semantics
    # (only the lower triangle is scaled and updated) are preserved.

```text
domain:
    # Matrix dimensions
    i: dim in [0, N)          # row index of C, A, B
    j: dim in [0, N)          # column index of C; only j <= i is updated (lower triangle)
    k: dim in [0, M)          # inner dimension (rank-2k)

data:
    # C is a full N x N matrix; we only update the lower triangle (j <= i).
    # Stored row-major so that j is the fast-varying (contiguous) index.
    C[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # A and B are N x M matrices.
    # We choose a column-major layout with respect to (i, k), i.e. k-major:
    #   - For fixed k and varying i (as in A[j, k] and B[j, k]) we get
    #     contiguous accesses, which is ideal when j is the innermost loop.
    #   - For fixed i and varying k (as in A[i, k] and B[i, k]) we still get
    #     stride-N accesses, acceptable inside a k-tile.
    A[i, k]: in DATA_TYPE = (i, k) -> k * N + i   # column-major in k
    B[i, k]: in DATA_TYPE = (i, k) -> k * N + i   # column-major in k

parameters:
    alpha: DATA_TYPE
    beta:  DATA_TYPE

    # Tunable blocking and vectorization parameters (chosen based on cache and SIMD width).
    TI: int    # tile size for i (e.g., 64)
    TJ: int    # tile size for j (e.g., 64)
    TK: int    # tile size for k (e.g., 64 or 128)
    VEC_J: int # SIMD width along j (e.g., 8 for AVX2 with float / 4 with double)
    UNROLL_K: int  # small unroll factor for the innermost k-loop inside a TK tile (e.g., 4)

computation:
    # Symmetric rank-2k update on the lower triangle of C:
    #   for i in 0..N-1
    #     for j in 0..i
    #       C[i][j] = beta * C[i][j]
    #       for k in 0..M-1
    #         C[i][j] += alpha * ( A[j][k] * B[i][k] + B[j][k] * A[i][k] )
    #
    # For j > i we leave C[i][j] unchanged.

    for i in [0, N), j in [0, N):
        if j <= i:
            C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j] +
                      alpha * sum(k in [0, M),
                                  A[j, k] * B[i, k] +
                                  B[j, k] * A[i, k])
        else:
            # Upper triangle: no-op, preserve initial C
            C[i, j] = C[i, j]

optimization:
    # --- Cache blocking (tiling) for better locality in C, A, and B ---

    # Tile i and j to operate on submatrices of C that fit into caches.
    # Tiles follow the triangular condition j <= i inside their bodies;
    # iterations with j > i become fast no-ops.
    block(i, I, TI)   # I indexes row tiles of size TI
    block(j, J, TJ)   # J indexes column tiles of size TJ

    # Tile k to reuse A[*, k] and B[*, k] across many (i, j) updates.
    block(k, K, TK)   # K indexes k-tiles of size TK

    # Hoist tile loops to the outermost levels to traverse C by blocks.
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)
    hoist(K)

    # --- Loop reordering for data reuse and triangular structure ---

    # Within each (I, J, K) tile, we favor an order:
    #   I (outer tiles of rows)
    #     J (tiles of columns)
    #       i (rows inside tile)
    #         K (k-tiles)
    #           k (within k-tile)
    #             j (columns inside tile, innermost)
    #
    # This makes j the innermost loop so that:
    #   - C[i, j] accesses are contiguous in memory (row-major C).
    #   - A[j, k] and B[j, k] use the column-major layout (k-major) for
    #     contiguous accesses over j when k is fixed.
    interchange(k, j)   # inside each (i, K) make k middle, j innermost

    # --- Parallelism ---

    # Parallelize across row tiles of C. Each (i, j) is updated independently
    # (subject to j <= i), so tiles along I can be computed in parallel
    # without synchronization.
    parallelize(I)

    # Optionally, when N is large, also parallelize across J for tiles that lie
    # fully within the lower triangle; J-parallelism should be chosen carefully
    # to avoid over-subscription and poor load balance.
    # parallelize(J)

    # --- Vectorization and unrolling ---

    # Vectorize the innermost j loop inside each tile so that we update
    # VEC_J consecutive elements of C[i, *] in a single SIMD operation.
    vectorize(j, VEC_J)

    # Unroll the inner k loop inside each TK-tile to increase ILP, while
    # keeping the unroll factor small enough to avoid register spilling.
    unroll(k, UNROLL_K)

    # --- Notes on correctness and structure ---
    # - The triangular condition j <= i is preserved explicitly in the
    #   computation; all loop transformations (blocking, interchange,
    #   parallelization, vectorization, unrolling) operate on an iteration
    #   space where iterations with j > i execute the cheap 'else' branch
    #   and leave C[i, j] unchanged.
    # - No extra large temporary buffers are introduced; A, B, and C are the
    #   only global arrays. Tiling operates on logical tiles in-place, so
    #   total memory usage is within the original footprint (< 1.5x).
```

```text
domain:
    i: dim in [0, N)      # Row index for C
    j: dim in [0, N)      # Column index for C
    k: dim in [0, M)      # Reduction index

data:
    # A and B are conceptually N×M (row i, column k), but we choose a
    # column-major physical layout so that accesses A[j,k], B[j,k]
    # (with j varying fastest) are unit-stride and vectorizable.
    A[i, k]: in DATA_TYPE = (i, k) -> k * N + i
        # column-major: for fixed k, A[*, k] is contiguous in memory.
    B[i, k]: in DATA_TYPE = (i, k) -> k * N + i
        # same column-major layout as A.

    # C is N×N, stored row-major so that C[i, *] is contiguous and we
    # can vectorize across j for a fixed i.
    C[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j
        # only the lower triangle (j <= i) is updated; the rest is left unchanged.

parameters:
    alpha: DATA_TYPE
    beta:  DATA_TYPE

computation:
    # Symmetric rank‑2k update on the lower triangle of C.
    # This fuses the original "scale" and "update" loops:
    #
    #   for i:
    #     for j <= i: C[i][j] *= beta;
    #     for k:
    #       for j <= i:
    #         C[i][j] += alpha*(A[j][k]*B[i][k] + B[j][k]*A[i][k]);
    #
    # into a single expression per (i,j) in the lower triangle.
    for i in [0, N), j in [0, N):
        if j <= i:
            C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j] +
                      alpha * sum(k in [0, M),
                                   A[j, k] * B[i, k] +
                                   B[j, k] * A[i, k])
        # For j > i, C[i, j] remains as initialized.

optimization:
    # -------------------------------
    # 1. Blocking / tiling in (i, j)
    # -------------------------------
    # Tile the (i, j) iteration space to improve cache locality for C and
    # for the A[j,k], B[j,k] rows used within each tile.
    #
    # TI, TJ are tunable tile sizes; good starting points on a modern
    # x64 with sizable L2/L3 caches might be 32 or 64.
    block(i, I, TI)    # i = I * TI + i_inner, 0 <= i_inner < TI
    block(j, J, TJ)    # j = J * TJ + j_inner, 0 <= j_inner < TJ

    # -------------------------------
    # 2. Blocking in the reduction (k)
    # -------------------------------
    # Tile the k dimension to increase data reuse from A/B in cache.
    # TK should be chosen so that:
    #   TI * TJ * TK * sizeof(DATA_TYPE)
    # fits comfortably in L2/L3. E.g., TK = 64 or 128.
    block(k, K, TK)

    # --------------------------------------------
    # 3. Skip tiles fully above the main diagonal
    # --------------------------------------------
    # The computation is only defined for j <= i, so any (I,J) tile
    # that satisfies "all its (i,j) pairs have j > i" can be skipped.
    #
    # Let:
    #   i_min = I * TI
    #   i_max = min((I+1)*TI - 1, N-1)
    #   j_min = J * TJ
    #   j_max = min((J+1)*TJ - 1, N-1)
    #
    # If j_min > i_max, then there is no (i,j) in this tile with j <= i.
    #
    # Pseudocode:
    #   for I:
    #     for J:
    #       if J*TJ > min((I+1)*TI - 1, N-1): continue
    #
    # We express this as a tile-level conditional.
    # (Syntax is descriptive; an implementation would lower this into
    # appropriate if-guards around the inner loops.)
    # for I, J:
    #     if (J*TJ) > min((I+1)*TI - 1, N-1): skip tile (I,J)

    # -------------------------------
    # 4. Loop ordering for locality
    # -------------------------------
    # Inside each (I,J) tile we want:
    #   outer:   i_inner  (rows of C)
    #   inner:   j_inner  (cols of C, contiguous in memory)
    #   innermost reduction: k (for sum)
    #
    # This gives:
    #   - C[i,j] accesses unit-stride in j (row-major).
    #   - A[j,k], B[j,k] accesses unit-stride in j (column-major).
    #
    # Ensure j varies faster than i within a tile.
    interchange(j, i)

    # -------------------------------
    # 5. Vectorization
    # -------------------------------
    # Vectorize across j_inner, which is unit-stride in both C and
    # in the dominant A[j,k], B[j,k] loads.
    #
    # V is chosen so that:
    #   V * sizeof(DATA_TYPE)
    # equals the SIMD width (e.g.,
    #   V = 8 for float32 with 256‑bit AVX,
    #   V = 4 for float64 with 256‑bit AVX).
    vectorize(j, V)

    # Optionally unroll a small factor of the k-tile to reduce reduction
    # loop overhead and expose more ILP; UK must divide TK.
    # This keeps temporary accumulators in registers.
    unroll(K, UK)

    # --------------------------------
    # 6. Parallelization over tiles
    # --------------------------------
    # Each (i,j) in the lower triangle is written exactly once and has
    # no dependence on other rows i'. Thus tiles in I (and J, subject to
    # the diagonal condition) are independent.
    #
    # Parallelize over I (row tiles); this yields coarse-grain tasks that
    # balance well across many cores.
    parallelize(I)
```
